catalog_quote: There are two hypothetical explanations for this unexpected result: in an early prehistoric stage of the language the laryngeal dropped in final position ... or the shift *e > a only worked on stressed position. However, neither is conclusive: more examples of such dropping are lacking and our knowledge of the nature and position of the Phrygian stress is insufficient.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Obrador-Cursach 2020 text we hold at p. 75, and both supporting remarks (p. 51 clitics; lexicon pp. 327-328 πατερης/πατρες) are where the record says. (2) The source is the 2020 Brill handbook, the standard and most comprehensive description of Phrygian; the held Ligorio & Lubotsky 2018 HSK sketch adds only 'presumably in pretonic position' for e/i vacillation and Wackernagel placement after 'the first accented word', neither giving a position rule. (3) The one newer work, Sorgo's 2026 Leiden dissertation 'A Historical Grammar of Phrygian', was downloaded (archive.org mirror of the Leiden repository PDF text) and its dedicated accent section states there is no direct evidence for accent placement, that it is unknown whether any limitation on accentable syllables existed, and that 'no firm conclusions can be made'; it reconstructs accent per word fr

sources.citation: Diakonoff, I. M. and V. P. Neroznak. 1985. Phrygian. Delmar, NY: Caravan Books. xx+149 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Passing assumption only, in a comparison with Armenian: 'a changeover from the I.-E. system of tones and mobile stress which apparently continued to obtain in Phrygian, to strong expiratory stress fixed on the penultimate syllable' [in Armenian]. Elsewhere stress is invoked ad hoc for vowel reflexes ('after stress *a, *e > [a?]'). No rule for Phrygian stress position is stated or argued.
sources.note: Glottolog-listed sketch (xx+149 pp.); only a passing assumption that IE mobile accent 'apparently continued' in Phrygian (p. 42); useful as the one older source that ventures a view.

sources.quote: p. 188: 'Neither the Old nor the New Phrygian scripts provide any way of marking an accent. Thus, there is no direct evidence for where the Phrygian accent would have been placed in a lexical word. ... the study of the Phrygian accentual system is still very much in its infancy. ...
